title: Virtual Memory, Paging and Memory Allocation
objectives: Explain how virtual addresses translate to physical addresses through multi-level page tables
Quantify TLB hits, page walks and minor/major page faults, and estimate TLB reach
Choose between read(), mmap() and huge pages for a given access pattern
Explain how demand paging and mlock create or remove tail latency in a trading hot path
motivation: The same binary runs in 8 microseconds in your backtest and 108 microseconds in production, once every few thousand ticks. Nothing in your code changed; the memory system did. Cold pages, TLB misses and unmlocked mappings are the invisible tax on hot paths, and virtual memory is the machinery behind every one of them.

blocks.md: Every pointer your program holds is **virtual**. The MMU translates it to a physical RAM address at every memory access, using page tables the kernel builds. Translation happens in fixed-size **pages**, 4 KiB on x86-64 by default, so a 48-bit virtual address splits into a 36-bit page number and a 12-bit offset, and the page number is looked up through a four-level table (four levels of 9 index bits each). Isolation between processes, demand paging and shared mappings all fall out of this one indirection.

blocks.tex: 48\text{-bit VA} \;=\; \underbrace{36\text{-bit VPN}}_{4 \times 9\text{-bit table indices}} \;+\; \underbrace{12\text{-bit offset}}_{4\,\text{KiB page}}
blocks.caption: Anatomy of a virtual address: the offset passes through unchanged; the page number indexes four page-table levels.

blocks.text: The TLB: translation with a cache

blocks.md: Walking four table levels per access would be fatal, so translations are cached in the **TLB**. A hit costs about a nanosecond; a miss forces a hardware **page walk**, up to four additional memory accesses, each slow if the table pages are cold. TLB capacity is quoted as *reach*: entries x page size. Huge pages (2 MiB, 1 GiB) multiply reach per entry, which is why a large order book backed by 2 MiB pages can dodge walks entirely.

blocks.title: Worked example: TLB reach
items: An L2 TLB has 2,048 entries; pages are 4 KiB, so each entry covers 4,096 bytes.
A 256 MiB working set accessed randomly: $8 / 256 = 3.125\%$ covered, nearly every access risks a multi-level walk.
With 2 MiB huge pages: $2{,}048 \times 2\ \text{MiB} = 4$ GiB of reach, the whole working set fits, and walks vanish.

blocks.title: The 100-microsecond surprise
blocks.md: One major page fault, the kernel pulling a cold page from disk or network storage, costs roughly 100 microseconds, ten times a typical 10 microsecond hot-path budget. This is why trading processes mlock() their hot data, pre-fault mappings with madvise(MADV_WILLNEED), and disable swap: the fault is not slow code, it is memory someone forgot to warm up.

A **minor fault** is cheap: the page is already in RAM (page cache, or a zero page about to be copied on write) and the kernel just wires the mapping in. A **major fault** needs real I/O, a file read or a swap-in, and that is the tail-latency bomb. **Demand paging** means the first touch pays: mmap a 64 MiB feed file and nothing is loaded until you read it, one 4 KiB page at a time.

blocks.caption: Map, prefetch, pin, then touch: faults get paid in warmup, not during trading hours. mlock needs RLIMIT_MEMLOCK, desks raise it deliberately.

blocks.text: Allocation: heap, mmap and the malloc threshold

blocks.md: User-space allocation rides on these mechanisms. malloc serves small requests from a heap it grows with brk; large requests (by default 128 KiB or more on glibc) get their own anonymous mmap, which is why freeing a huge block returns memory to the OS immediately while freeing small blocks leaves it pooled in the heap. Anonymous pages are zero-filled lazily on first touch; file-backed pages come from the page cache and are shared by every process mapping the same file.

This is also the zero-copy argument. Reading the same market-data file with read() copies every byte from page cache into your buffer; mmap gives every process a window onto the same physical pages, and the copies disappear. At a million messages per second the copies are the cost. The trade-offs, first-touch faults, TLB pressure from long mappings, mlock limits, are exactly what the exercises price.

guidedExercise.prompt: A risk engine randomly reads a 64 MiB working set out of a 2 GiB file mapping. The L2 TLB has 1,536 entries and pages are 4 KiB. (a) Compute the TLB reach in MiB. (b) What fraction of the working set fits, as a percentage? (c) Recompute (a) with 2 MiB huge pages and state the consequence.
hints: 1536 x 4 KiB in KiB first, then convert to MiB.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $1{,}536 \times 4\ \text{KiB} = 6{,}144\ \text{KiB} = 6$ MiB. (b) $6 / 64 = 9.375\%$ - over 90% of accesses risk a multi-level walk. (c) $1{,}536 \times 2\ \text{MiB} = 3{,}072\ \text{MiB} = 3$ GiB, which covers the entire 2 GiB set: the walks (and their ~100 ns each) disappear.

independentExercise.prompt: A warmup pass scans a 512 MiB mmap'd capture that is fully cold (not in the page cache). Assume every first touch is a major fault costing ~100 microseconds. (a) How many faults occur? (b) What does the warmup cost in seconds? (c) Roughly what does the second pass cost if the machine has enough RAM? (d) Which two syscalls would you add to make warmup explicit?
hints: Faults x 100 microseconds, converted to seconds.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $512 \times 1024 / 4 = 131{,}072$ pages, so 131,072 major faults. (b) $131{,}072 \times 100\,\mu s = 13.1$ s of fault cost. (c) Roughly zero extra fault cost, pages are resident and TLB-warmed, so the pass runs at memory speed. (d) madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) to prefetch and mlock() to keep the range resident.

commonMistakes: Confusing virtual size with resident memory: a 64 MiB mapping costs nothing until touched; RSS is the truth.
Assuming malloc(size) commits memory, anonymous pages are zero-filled lazily on first touch.
Blaming 'slow RAM' for a 100 microsecond outlier: that is a major fault, not a cache miss (cache misses are ~100 ns).
Calling free() and expecting RSS to drop for small allocations, heap space is pooled, not returned.
realWorldApplication: Databases, JVMs and storage engines all manage page faults, huge pages and mmap windows; every profiler trace showing a mystery 100 microsecond stall is this lesson in production.
quantFinanceApplication: mmap'd tick files, mlocked order books and huge-page-backed matching engines are standard desk practice; each exists to keep the ~100 microsecond major fault and the ~100 ns TLB miss out of a 10 microsecond budget.
summary: Virtual addresses translate through multi-level page tables cached in the TLB; a 48-bit VA = 36-bit VPN + 12-bit offset for 4 KiB pages.
The costs are different orders of magnitude: TLB hit ~1 ns, page walk ~100 ns, minor fault ~microseconds, major fault ~100 microseconds.
TLB reach = entries x page size; huge pages multiply reach and kill walks on large working sets.
Demand paging makes the first touch pay; madvise and mlock move that payment into controlled warmup.
Large mallocs are anonymous mmaps (freed straight back to the OS); small allocations live in the pooled heap.

quiz.prompt: On a TLB miss where the requested page IS present in RAM, what happens next?
options: Hardware performs a multi-level page walk to build the translation
The page is copied into the TLB from disk
The kernel switches processes to free memory
The CPU raises a page fault for the kernel to fix
quiz.explanation: Present pages never need the kernel: hardware walks the four-level table itself and caches the result in the TLB. Only a *not-present* page escalates to a fault.

quiz.prompt: How many distinct 4 KiB pages are touched when you scan a 64 MiB mapping end to end once?
quiz.explanation: 64 MiB = 65,536 KiB; 65,536 / 4 = 16,384 pages, so demand paging can fault up to 16,384 times on first touch.

quiz.prompt: An L2 TLB has 4,096 entries and the process uses 2 MiB huge pages. What is the TLB reach, in GiB?
quiz.explanation: 4,096 x 2 MiB = 8,192 MiB = 8 GiB; a working set under 8 GiB then fits in the TLB with no walks.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about page faults are true?
options: A major fault requires reading data from disk or network storage
mlock() keeps covered pages resident so they cannot fault again
A minor fault means the page had to be fetched from swap
A TLB hit and a TLB miss cost about the same
quiz.explanation: Major faults are I/O-bound; mlock pins pages resident so they cannot fault again while locked. Minor faults are page-cache/zero-page work, not swap; and a TLB miss costs roughly 100x a hit.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python script print?
quiz.code:
PAGE = 4096
mapped = 64 * 1024 * 1024      # 64 MiB mmap
pages = mapped // PAGE         # first touch faults once per page
print(pages)
print(pages * PAGE == mapped)
quiz.explanation: 67,108,864 bytes / 4,096 = 16,384 pages exactly, so the mapping is a whole number of pages and the check prints True.

quiz.prompt: Why does freeing a very large heap block usually return memory to the OS immediately, while freeing small blocks may not?
quiz.modelAnswer: glibc malloc serves large requests (default 128 KiB and above) from dedicated anonymous mmaps, so free() can munmap them straight back to the kernel. Small allocations live inside the brk-managed heap, which can only be released at its top, so freed space stays pooled to avoid fragmentation.
quiz.explanation: The 128 KiB default mmap threshold splits the two regimes; below it, memory is recycled inside the heap rather than returned.

flashcards.back: $48 = 36\ \text{VPN bits} + 12\ \text{offset bits}$; the 36 VPN bits index 4 levels of 9 bits each.
Minor: page already in RAM (page cache or zero page), kernel wires the mapping, ~microseconds. Major: real I/O from disk/swap, ~100 microseconds or worse, a tail-latency hazard.
$\text{reach} = \text{entries} \times \text{page size}$: 2,048 entries x 4 KiB = 8 MiB; the same entries x 2 MiB pages = 4 GiB.
Zero-copy shared access to page-cache pages, demand-paged on touch, controllable via madvise/mlock, versus read()'s copy per call.
